figures.caption: Figure 2. Representation of batch effects in microscopy imaging data considered as a multi-source domain adaptation (MSDA) problem. In this setting, each source consists of different experimental conditions, e.g. different plates. In each domain, an image of the same class is depicted, which represents a particular mechanism-of-action (MoA). Control samples are unperturbed samples, that are present in every domain, and which we represent with the c symbol.

Table 1. MoA prediction accuracy on in-domain and unseen experimental batches from a new domain. Column "TTA" indicates that the method can adapt itself given samples from a new domain at test time, i.e. test time adaptation. “In-context” means that the model adapts its parameters based on the test samples through in-context learning. The accuracy values denote mean and standard deviation over 5-fold cross-validation, thus five training re-runs of each method. "FM" indicates a foundation model.

Table 4. Comparison of MoA classification accuracy of different methods across target sources (S8, S3, and S6) under different degrees of label shift. A lower α denotes a higher degree of label shift. The accuracy values denote mean and standard deviation over re-runs with three different seeds.

Table 2. Comparison of MoA classification accuracy of different methods across target sources. The element before the arrow indicates the training domain, the element after the arrow indicates the evaluation domain. The accuracy values denote the mean and standard deviation over 3 re-runs with different seeds.

Figure 3. Graphic representation of our method, CS-ARM-BN, and comparison to ARM-BN (Zhang et al., 2021). Both are meta-learning methods that are be modified at test-time by using the BN statistics from the target domain (lilac). CS-ARM-BN uses control samples both at training and at inference time, which provides stability when (b) the number of perturbed samples is small or (c) the label distribution is shifted.
